edge.title: The screenshot that isn't money
edge.setup: You're selling a phone, or you run a small counter. The buyer holds up a UPI success screen — right amount, right name, a reference number, 'bank server is slow, it'll reflect in an hour'. They're already walking away with the goods. There are apps whose only purpose is generating that screen.
edge.tell: Confirmation came from their screen, not from your bank.
move: Only your own SMS, bank app balance, or payment-device voice alert counts. Nothing on their phone is evidence.
Say the sentence plainly: 'I'll hand it over when my bank confirms.' It is not rude; it's the norm.
For sales, meet inside a bank branch or a busy shop — not a parking lot.
edge.why: Trust normally travels with money. Screenshots break that link by making the proof forgeable and instant. Every defence restores the link: confirmation must arrive through a channel the other person cannot author.
edge.variants: Same shape: forged NEFT receipts, fake courier-dispatch proofs, 'payment initiated' emails from a lookalike domain.

scenario.question: You are selling your old phone to a buyer from an online listing, meeting outside a mall in Bengaluru. He shows you a UPI success screen with the right amount, your name and a reference number, says his bank's server is slow and it will reflect in an hour, and reaches for the phone. Your own bank app shows nothing yet. What do you do?

choices.text: Keep hold of the phone and say you will hand it over when your own bank app or SMS confirms the money. Nothing on his screen counts.
Hand it over. The screen has the right amount, your name and a reference number, and delays do happen.
Photograph his screen and his face as proof, then hand it over.
Take his ID card as security and let him go with the phone until the money arrives.

lens.name: Asymmetric information
lens.one_line: When one side knows much more than the other, the market degrades toward the worse goods.
lens.detail: If buyers can't tell good used cars from bad, they offer an average price. Owners of genuinely good cars refuse to sell at that price and leave the market, so the average quality drops, so the price drops further. Quality collapses — not from dishonesty, but from unverifiability. Every real fix is a verification mechanism: warranties, certification, inspection, reputation.
elsewhere: Freelance marketplaces race to the bottom without reviews.
Insurance pools get sicker when only the sick buy in.
A degree works partly as a costly signal of something an employer can't directly see.
lens.test: What can the other side see that I can't — and what would make it visible?
lens.today: Moneycontrol reports Visa, Mastercard and JPMorgan have disclosed customer data exposure through a cyberattack on a third-party vendor. You cannot see which vendors hold your details or what leaked, but whoever took them can, so a caller who knows your card number or recent spends has proved nothing about who they are. The fix is the one this model always points to: verify through a channel they cannot control, such as the number printed on your card.

carry_over.answer: You are being asked to answer for contents you cannot verify, for a person who will not be there if it goes wrong.
